questions.prompt: In a user-level many-to-one thread model, one thread makes a blocking system call. What is the usual effect?
options: The entire process may block
Only the calling thread is guaranteed to block
A new kernel thread is created automatically
The call is converted to nonblocking I/O
answer: The entire process may block
questions.explanation: The kernel schedules the process as a unit in a many-to-one model. A blocking call can therefore prevent every user thread in that process from running.

questions.prompt: A many-to-one runtime has four runnable user threads but only one kernel-scheduled execution context. How many of these threads can execute simultaneously on two CPUs?
options: At most one
Two
Four
Zero
answer: At most one
questions.explanation: All user threads share one kernel execution context, so only one can be executing at a time. Multiple CPUs do not provide parallelism for this process under many-to-one mapping.

questions.prompt: A one-to-one model maps each user thread to a kernel thread. Which advantage follows most directly?
options: A blocking call by one thread need not block its siblings
Thread creation has zero kernel cost
All threads share separate address spaces
The kernel does not schedule threads
answer: A blocking call by one thread need not block its siblings
questions.explanation: With separate kernel-schedulable entities, another thread can run while one blocks, subject to available CPU and other constraints.

questions.prompt: A program has 8 runnable threads under one-to-one mapping on a machine with 4 CPUs. What is the maximum number that can execute simultaneously?
questions.explanation: Execution in parallel is bounded by the number of available CPUs, so no more than four of the eight runnable threads can execute at once.

questions.prompt: Which resources are normally shared by threads of the same process?
options: Global variables and open file descriptors
Stack and register set
Thread ID and program counter
Signal mask and stack in all models
answer: Global variables and open file descriptors
questions.explanation: Threads share process resources such as address space and open descriptors, while each thread needs its own stack and CPU execution state.

questions.prompt: Which state must be distinct for each concurrently executing thread?
options: Program counter and register set
Executable code pages
Process-wide heap
Current working directory
answer: Program counter and register set
questions.explanation: Each thread has its own execution point and registers. Code and heap belong to the shared process address space.

questions.prompt: A mutex protects a shared counter. Two threads increment it using a non-atomic read-modify-write sequence without locking. What can happen?
options: An increment can be lost
The counter must increase by exactly two
The threads receive different address spaces
The kernel serializes all user instructions
answer: An increment can be lost
questions.explanation: Interleaving can let both threads read the same old value and then write the same incremented value, losing one update.

questions.prompt: A thread yields the CPU voluntarily but remains runnable. Which transition describes it?
options: running to ready
running to blocked
ready to terminated
blocked to running
answer: running to ready
questions.explanation: Yield relinquishes the current CPU turn without waiting for an event or ending execution, so the thread returns to a runnable state.

questions.prompt: A thread waits on a condition variable. What should it normally do after waking?
options: Recheck the predicate while holding the associated mutex
Assume the predicate is true
Use the condition variable as a mutex
Exit because wakeups are spurious
answer: Recheck the predicate while holding the associated mutex
questions.explanation: Condition-variable wakeups can be spurious or another thread can consume the condition first. The thread must recheck its predicate in a loop under the mutex.

questions.prompt: A process with multiple threads calls exec successfully. What normally happens to the old threads?
options: The process image is replaced and the old threads cease to exist
They continue in the old image
Only the caller changes image and siblings keep running
Each thread becomes a separate process
answer: The process image is replaced and the old threads cease to exist
questions.explanation: Exec replaces the process image as a whole. The old execution context, including its threads, is discarded as the new program starts.

questions.prompt: In a many-to-many model, many user threads are multiplexed over several kernel threads. Which statement is true?
options: The number of executing threads is limited by kernel threads and CPUs
Every user thread must have a dedicated kernel thread
A blocking call must block all user threads
The model forbids parallel execution
answer: The number of executing threads is limited by kernel threads and CPUs
questions.explanation: Several kernel threads permit parallel execution and allow user threads to be multiplexed. Actual simultaneous execution cannot exceed available kernel contexts or CPUs.

questions.prompt: A thread library implements user-level scheduling, and the kernel sees one schedulable entity. Which scheduling decision is generally invisible to the kernel?
options: Which user thread runs next within the process
Which process receives a CPU
Which address space is active
Which kernel thread is preempted
answer: Which user thread runs next within the process
questions.explanation: The user runtime chooses among its user threads. The kernel sees and schedules the single underlying kernel entity, not the runtime?s internal selection.

questions.prompt: A thread is preempted while holding a mutex. What is generally true?
options: The mutex remains locked until an owner releases it
The scheduler automatically releases it
All waiting threads enter the critical section
The process must terminate
answer: The mutex remains locked until an owner releases it
questions.explanation: Preemption changes which thread runs, not lock ownership. Other threads remain excluded until the owner unlocks or a recovery protocol intervenes.

questions.prompt: A thread exits normally while other threads in the process continue. What is the expected process-level outcome?
options: The process can remain alive while its other threads run
The entire process must terminate
All threads become zombies
The address space is destroyed immediately
answer: The process can remain alive while its other threads run
questions.explanation: Thread termination is distinct from process termination. The process remains active as long as it has other live threads or otherwise continues.

questions.prompt: A program creates 5 threads that are all CPU-bound on a 2-CPU machine. Ignoring other work, what is the maximum simultaneous parallelism?
questions.explanation: At most one thread can execute per CPU at a time. Five runnable threads are time-shared across the two CPUs.

questions.prompt: Which statement distinguishes concurrency from parallelism?
options: Concurrent tasks can make progress in overlapping time; parallel tasks execute simultaneously
Concurrency requires multiple CPUs; parallelism does not
They are identical terms
Parallelism occurs only with user-level threads
answer: Concurrent tasks can make progress in overlapping time; parallel tasks execute simultaneously
questions.explanation: Concurrency concerns overlapping progress and can occur by interleaving on one CPU. Parallelism specifically requires simultaneous execution.

questions.prompt: A thread accesses a thread-local variable. Which property is intended?
options: Each thread has its own instance of that variable
The variable is shared process-wide
The variable is stored only in the kernel
The variable cannot be modified
answer: Each thread has its own instance of that variable
questions.explanation: Thread-local storage provides a separate instance per thread, despite the shared process address space.

questions.prompt: A process contains two threads that concurrently call a non-reentrant library function using one static buffer. What is the main risk?
options: Their calls may corrupt or overwrite shared intermediate state
Each call receives a private copy automatically
The kernel serializes all library calls
The process forks on each call
answer: Their calls may corrupt or overwrite shared intermediate state
questions.explanation: A static buffer is shared by both threads. Interleaved calls can overwrite one another?s state unless the library uses synchronization or per-thread storage.

questions.prompt: A thread waits for a lock held by another thread that is itself waiting for the first thread to signal it. What condition can result?
options: Deadlock
Starvation freedom
Parallel speedup
A race-free atomic update
answer: Deadlock
questions.explanation: The circular dependency prevents either thread from making progress: each waits for an action that the other cannot perform while blocked.

questions.prompt: In a user-level threading system with one kernel thread, a page fault that blocks the kernel thread may:
options: block all user threads in that process
block only the faulting user thread in every implementation
create an extra CPU
make the page fault disappear
answer: block all user threads in that process
questions.explanation: The kernel blocks the single kernel execution context while servicing the fault, so the user scheduler cannot run its other threads until it resumes.

questions.prompt: A kernel supports thread preemption, but a user-level library does not expose parallel execution. Which is most likely?
options: Many-to-one mapping
One-to-one mapping
Many-to-many mapping with multiple kernel threads
Separate process per user thread
answer: Many-to-one mapping
questions.explanation: If many user threads map to only one kernel thread, kernel preemption can preempt that entity but cannot run two of the user threads simultaneously.

questions.prompt: A thread calls fork in a multithreaded process. Which child state is typical in POSIX semantics?
options: Only the calling thread is present in the child
Every parent thread is duplicated and scheduled
The child has no address space
The child immediately shares the parent PID
answer: Only the calling thread is present in the child
questions.explanation: The child receives a copy-on-write process image but only the forking thread survives as a thread. Other threads are absent from the child.

questions.prompt: A thread has its own stack. Why is a separate stack needed?
options: Each thread has independent call frames and return addresses
Stacks contain the shared executable code
The kernel requires every stack to be shared
A stack stores the process PID only
answer: Each thread has independent call frames and return addresses
questions.explanation: Independent execution paths require independent activation records, local variables, and return addresses. Sharing one stack would corrupt nested calls.

questions.prompt: A worker pool has 12 threads, but only 3 tasks are ready. How many workers can be actively executing useful tasks at most?
questions.explanation: Only three tasks are available, so at most three workers can execute useful task work concurrently. CPU count may reduce this further.

questions.prompt: A thread blocks on a system call in a one-to-one model. Another thread in the same process is runnable. What is generally possible?
options: The scheduler can run the other thread
The blocked thread must be spun until I/O completes
All threads share one program counter
The process address space must be copied
answer: The scheduler can run the other thread
questions.explanation: A separate kernel thread can be scheduled independently, allowing the runnable sibling to use a CPU while the first waits.

questions.prompt: Which statement about thread context switching is correct?
options: It saves the outgoing thread?s register state and selects another runnable thread
It always switches to a different process
It necessarily copies the shared heap
It discards the outgoing stack
answer: It saves the outgoing thread?s register state and selects another runnable thread
questions.explanation: The thread?s execution state must be saved so it can resume. A switch may stay within the same process and preserve shared memory.

questions.prompt: Two threads share a file descriptor and issue reads concurrently. What is a possible source of nondeterminism?
options: Their operations may interleave and advance a shared file offset
Each thread automatically receives an independent offset
The descriptor changes their PIDs
Reads are always globally ordered by creation time
answer: Their operations may interleave and advance a shared file offset
questions.explanation: After descriptor inheritance or sharing, the same open-file description can carry a shared offset. Concurrent reads can affect which bytes each obtains.

questions.prompt: Thread A holds mutex M and waits for a condition. It calls condition_wait(M). What must this operation do atomically with respect to waiting?
options: Release M and begin waiting
Keep M locked forever
Destroy M
Wake every thread and retain M
answer: Release M and begin waiting
questions.explanation: Condition-wait releases the associated mutex as it blocks, preventing a missed signal window; it reacquires the mutex before returning.

questions.prompt: A condition variable is signaled when no thread is waiting. What is generally true?
options: The signal is not a stored permit for a future waiter
The next waiter is guaranteed to consume it
The mutex becomes permanently locked
The process terminates
answer: The signal is not a stored permit for a future waiter
questions.explanation: Condition variables notify current waiters; unlike semaphores, they do not generally retain a count of signals for future waiters.

questions.prompt: A semaphore is initialized to 3 and four threads each successfully perform wait once, with no signal operations. How many threads can pass the wait?
questions.explanation: Each successful wait consumes one unit. Three permits allow three threads to proceed; the fourth blocks until a signal adds a permit.

questions.prompt: A process has 6 runnable threads under many-to-one mapping on a 1-CPU system. If the CPU is idle, how many can execute now?
questions.explanation: The process has one kernel-schedulable entity, so at most one user thread can run at a time. An idle CPU can execute that entity.

questions.prompt: A process has 6 runnable threads under one-to-one mapping on a 3-CPU system. What is the maximum simultaneous execution count?
questions.explanation: Each user thread maps to a kernel thread, but the machine has only three CPUs. Thus at most three threads can execute simultaneously.

questions.prompt: A multithreaded server has 10 requests but a pool of 4 workers. Assuming all requests are independent and CPUs are abundant, how many requests can be processed at once?
questions.explanation: Only four worker threads can service requests concurrently. The other six requests must wait for a worker to become available.

questions.prompt: A mutex has one owner and three waiting threads. When the owner unlocks, which fact is guaranteed by the mutex abstraction alone?
options: At most one thread acquires ownership at a time
All three waiters acquire it simultaneously
The oldest waiter always wins
The owner is terminated
answer: At most one thread acquires ownership at a time
questions.explanation: Mutual exclusion guarantees a single owner. Fairness and waiter ordering depend on the implementation and are not guaranteed by the basic abstraction.

questions.prompt: A thread acquires a non-recursive mutex and then attempts to lock it again. What is the common outcome?
options: It blocks or deadlocks waiting for itself
It acquires a second independent copy
The mutex becomes a semaphore
The process forks
answer: It blocks or deadlocks waiting for itself
questions.explanation: A non-recursive mutex cannot be acquired twice by the same owner. The second acquisition commonly deadlocks or reports an error, depending on its type.

questions.prompt: A program uses a spinlock while the lock holder is descheduled for a long time on a single CPU. What is a likely effect?
options: The waiting thread wastes CPU while the owner cannot run
The owner releases the lock automatically
The waiting thread sleeps without consuming CPU
The system guarantees immediate ownership transfer
answer: The waiting thread wastes CPU while the owner cannot run
questions.explanation: Spinning consumes the only CPU while the descheduled owner needs that CPU to run and release the lock. Blocking locks avoid this waste for long waits.

questions.prompt: When is a spinlock often preferable to a blocking mutex?
options: For very short critical sections where sleeping costs more than spinning
Whenever a critical section can block on I/O
When a lock may be held indefinitely
When there is only one process
answer: For very short critical sections where sleeping costs more than spinning
questions.explanation: A brief expected hold time can make spinning cheaper than sleep/wakeup overhead. A lock held across blocking work makes spinning wasteful.

questions.prompt: A thread pool has 8 workers and a queue of 20 independent jobs. If each worker executes at most one job at a time, how many jobs can be running simultaneously?
options: At most 8
At most 20
At most 28
Exactly 1
answer: At most 8
questions.explanation: Each worker can run one job concurrently, so eight workers cap running jobs at eight. Queue size affects waiting work, not active capacity.

questions.prompt: A barrier is configured for 5 threads. Four arrive and wait; the fifth arrives. What is the expected barrier behavior?
options: All five are released to continue
Only the fifth proceeds
The first four terminate
The barrier count becomes 6
answer: All five are released to continue
questions.explanation: A barrier releases participants once the configured number of arrivals has occurred. The fifth arrival completes the phase and lets all five proceed.

questions.prompt: A barrier participant exits before arriving, leaving only four arrivals for a five-thread barrier. What is the likely result absent cancellation/reconfiguration?
options: The other threads can wait indefinitely
The barrier releases after a timeout of zero
The exited thread is recreated
The barrier becomes a mutex
answer: The other threads can wait indefinitely
questions.explanation: The required arrival count is never reached, so the remaining participants can block indefinitely. Robust designs handle cancellation or participant failure.

questions.prompt: A thread executes an atomic fetch-and-add on a shared counter. Which property does atomicity provide?
options: The read-modify-write appears indivisible to competing threads
The operation is guaranteed to be fair
The counter cannot overflow
The entire process becomes serial
answer: The read-modify-write appears indivisible to competing threads
questions.explanation: Atomicity prevents interleaving inside the update, avoiding lost increments. It does not by itself guarantee fairness, no overflow, or serialization of unrelated work.

questions.prompt: Two threads update different variables on different cache lines without synchronization. Must this be a data race?
options: Not necessarily; distinct memory locations avoid a conflicting access
Yes, any concurrent writes are a race
No, threads cannot execute concurrently
Yes, because they share a process
answer: Not necessarily; distinct memory locations avoid a conflicting access
questions.explanation: A data race requires conflicting unsynchronized accesses to the same memory location under the language?s model. Separate variables can be independent.

questions.prompt: Two threads concurrently write the same non-atomic variable, and at least one write is not synchronized. What is the core issue?
options: A data race and potentially undefined behavior in languages such as C/C++
A deadlock is guaranteed
The kernel merges the values
A context switch is disabled
answer: A data race and potentially undefined behavior in languages such as C/C++
questions.explanation: Unsynchronized conflicting accesses constitute a data race. In C and C++, a data race on ordinary memory yields undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: Thread A signals a condition variable before Thread B begins waiting. What should the program rely on?
options: A shared predicate protected by a mutex, not the signal being remembered
The signal is stored until B waits
B must wake at process startup
A must hold the mutex forever
answer: A shared predicate protected by a mutex, not the signal being remembered
questions.explanation: Condition signals are not stored as permits. The predicate records the condition; B checks it under the mutex and waits only if needed.

questions.prompt: A counting semaphore starts at zero. One thread signals it, then another thread waits. What happens to the wait?
options: It can consume the stored permit and proceed
It blocks forever because it missed the signal
It decrements below zero and terminates
It creates a new semaphore
answer: It can consume the stored permit and proceed
questions.explanation: A semaphore retains its count. The signal increments it, so a later wait can consume that permit and proceed immediately.

questions.prompt: A binary semaphore starts at one. Two threads call wait concurrently. How many can pass before any signal?
options: Unlimited
questions.explanation: The initial permit is consumed by one successful wait. The second call must wait until a signal restores the permit.

questions.prompt: A thread is canceled while holding a mutex and has no cleanup handler. What is a possible consequence?
options: The mutex can remain locked and block other threads
The OS always unlocks every user mutex
All other threads inherit the mutex
The process is guaranteed to recover its invariant
answer: The mutex can remain locked and block other threads
questions.explanation: Cancellation does not necessarily release application-level locks safely. Without cleanup or robust recovery, other threads may block and shared state may be inconsistent.

questions.prompt: Deferred cancellation is requested for a thread. When is cancellation normally acted upon?
options: At a cancellation point or explicit cancellation check
Immediately after every machine instruction
Only after the process exits
Only when another process forks
answer: At a cancellation point or explicit cancellation check
questions.explanation: Deferred cancellation waits until the target reaches a defined cancellation point or checks its status, allowing cleanup at controlled locations.

questions.prompt: A thread holds a lock and is asynchronously canceled at an arbitrary instruction. Why is this dangerous?
options: It may leave locks held and shared data partially updated
It always completes the critical section
It cannot be canceled while running
The kernel rolls back its writes
answer: It may leave locks held and shared data partially updated
questions.explanation: Arbitrary cancellation can interrupt an invariant-preserving sequence at any point, leaving inconsistent data or unreleased locks.

questions.prompt: A process is CPU-bound with four threads, but all threads share a global lock around the entire computation. What is the likely speedup on four CPUs?
options: Little or none because the lock serializes the work
Exactly fourfold
Infinite
At least twofold
answer: Little or none because the lock serializes the work
questions.explanation: A lock around the whole computation allows only one thread into the work region at a time. The CPU-bound workload is therefore effectively serialized.

questions.prompt: A process has 7 runnable user threads under many-to-one mapping. How many can execute simultaneously on an 8-CPU machine?
questions.explanation: Many-to-one mapping exposes one kernel-schedulable entity. Even with eight CPUs, only one of its user threads can execute at a time.

questions.prompt: A process has 9 runnable threads under one-to-one mapping and 6 available CPUs. What is the maximum number of simultaneously executing threads?
questions.explanation: One-to-one mapping allows kernel scheduling of each thread, but execution is still bounded by available CPUs. The maximum is min(9,6) = 6.

questions.prompt: A counting semaphore begins at 4. Six wait operations occur, with no signals. How many wait calls complete immediately?
questions.explanation: The initial count provides four permits. Four waits consume them; the remaining two must block.

questions.prompt: A binary semaphore begins at 0. Five signals occur, then three waits occur. What is its count after these operations, assuming a counting semaphore rather than a capped binary implementation?
questions.explanation: Starting from zero, five signals add five permits and three waits consume three, leaving count two. A strictly capped binary semaphore would have different semantics; the question specifies counting behavior.

questions.prompt: A condition variable has 3 waiting threads. One signal is issued. How many waiting threads is the signal intended to wake?
questions.explanation: A signal generally wakes one waiter, if one is waiting. A broadcast would be used to wake all three.

questions.prompt: A barrier requires 6 arrivals. If 5 threads have arrived, how many additional arrivals are needed to release it?
questions.explanation: The threshold is six. With five arrivals, exactly one more participant must arrive.

questions.prompt: A thread context switch costs 2 microseconds. Switching from thread A to B and later from B back to A costs how many microseconds total?
questions.explanation: There are two context switches, each costing two microseconds. The combined overhead is 2 ? 2 = 4 microseconds.

questions.prompt: Eight threads each increment a shared counter 100 times using a correct mutex. What is the final counter increase from an initial value of zero?
questions.explanation: The mutex prevents lost updates, so all 8 ? 100 increments take effect. The final increase is 800.

questions.prompt: Four threads each perform 50 atomic increments on a shared counter. What is the final value from an initial zero?
questions.explanation: Atomic fetch-and-add preserves every update. The total is 4 ? 50 = 200.

questions.prompt: A process has 3 threads and 2 CPUs. If all are runnable and CPU-bound, what is the maximum simultaneous execution count?
questions.explanation: The CPU count limits parallel execution. Although three threads are runnable, at most two can execute on two CPUs at once.

questions.prompt: A pool has 10 worker threads and 7 independent ready tasks. How many tasks can be actively assigned to workers at most?
questions.explanation: Only seven tasks are available. Even though there are ten workers, no more than seven can perform those tasks simultaneously.

questions.prompt: A pool has 10 worker threads and 12 CPUs, with 16 independent ready tasks. What is the maximum number of tasks executing simultaneously?
questions.explanation: The worker count is the bottleneck: at most ten tasks can be assigned concurrently, even though there are more CPUs and tasks.

questions.prompt: A semaphore count is 2. Three waits occur, then one signal. How many waits can have completed by the end?
questions.explanation: Two waits consume the initial permits; the third blocks. The signal adds a permit and allows that third wait to complete.

questions.prompt: A process has 5 threads. Each thread requires a 16 KiB stack. What is the total stack allocation, ignoring guard pages and metadata, in KiB?
questions.explanation: The per-thread stack requirement is 16 KiB. For five threads, 5 ? 16 = 80 KiB.

questions.prompt: A system can run 4 kernel threads in parallel. A many-to-many process has 12 runnable user threads mapped over those 4 kernel threads. What is the maximum simultaneous execution count?
questions.explanation: The user threads are multiplexed over four kernel execution contexts. Even if all twelve are runnable, no more than four can execute simultaneously.

questions.prompt: Which statements about threads in one process are generally correct?
options: They share the process address space
Each thread has its own program counter
Each thread has its own stack
Each thread must have a distinct executable image
answer: They share the process address space
Each thread has its own program counter
Each thread has its own stack
questions.explanation: Threads share the process image, but each needs private execution state such as program counter, registers, and stack. They do not each require a separate executable image.

questions.prompt: Which are advantages commonly associated with multithreading?
options: Responsiveness while another thread blocks
Potential parallelism on multiple CPUs
Lower-cost communication through shared address space
Automatic elimination of data races
answer: Responsiveness while another thread blocks
Potential parallelism on multiple CPUs
Lower-cost communication through shared address space
questions.explanation: Threads can preserve responsiveness, use multiple CPUs, and communicate through shared memory. Shared state makes races possible, so synchronization remains necessary.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe many-to-one threading?
options: Many user threads map to one kernel thread
A blocking system call may block all user threads
The process cannot use multiple CPUs in parallel through those threads
Each user thread is independently preempted by the kernel
answer: Many user threads map to one kernel thread
A blocking system call may block all user threads
The process cannot use multiple CPUs in parallel through those threads
questions.explanation: The kernel sees one entity, so blocking can stall all user threads and parallel execution is unavailable. The kernel cannot independently preempt each user thread.

questions.prompt: Which statements about one-to-one threading are correct?
options: Each user thread maps to a kernel thread
A blocked thread may leave sibling threads runnable
Kernel resource use can grow with thread count
It inherently guarantees fairness among threads
answer: Each user thread maps to a kernel thread
A blocked thread may leave sibling threads runnable
Kernel resource use can grow with thread count
questions.explanation: One-to-one provides independent kernel scheduling and can allow siblings to run when one blocks, but incurs kernel resources. Fairness is not automatic.

questions.prompt: Which practices help avoid lost updates to shared state?
options: Protect the update with a mutex
Use a suitable atomic read-modify-write operation
Ensure all access is correctly synchronized
Add a sleep between the read and write
answer: Protect the update with a mutex
Use a suitable atomic read-modify-write operation
Ensure all access is correctly synchronized
questions.explanation: A mutex or atomic operation makes the update indivisible or mutually exclusive. Sleeping does not establish synchronization and cannot make a race correct.

questions.prompt: Which statements about mutexes are correct?
options: They provide mutual exclusion when used consistently
A mutex should normally be unlocked by its owner
A mutex alone does not guarantee fairness
Unlocking allows several owners at once
answer: They provide mutual exclusion when used consistently
A mutex should normally be unlocked by its owner
A mutex alone does not guarantee fairness
questions.explanation: A mutex enforces one owner at a time; ownership rules generally require the owner to release it. Fairness depends on implementation, and unlock does not create multiple owners.

questions.prompt: Which statements about semaphores are correct?
options: A counting semaphore can represent multiple permits
A wait operation consumes a permit when available
A signal can add a permit
A condition-variable signal is always stored like a semaphore permit
answer: A counting semaphore can represent multiple permits
A wait operation consumes a permit when available
A signal can add a permit
questions.explanation: Counting semaphores retain permit counts, consumed by wait and increased by signal. Condition-variable signals generally are not remembered for future waiters.

questions.prompt: Which are valid reasons for waiting on a condition variable in a loop?
options: Spurious wakeups can occur
Another thread can change the predicate before the waiter reacquires the mutex
A wakeup does not itself guarantee that the desired condition holds
The loop causes the scheduler to terminate the process
answer: Spurious wakeups can occur
Another thread can change the predicate before the waiter reacquires the mutex
A wakeup does not itself guarantee that the desired condition holds
questions.explanation: Wakeup only prompts the thread to recheck shared state. Spurious wakeups and competing consumers mean the predicate must be checked again under its mutex.

questions.prompt: Which statements about thread cancellation are correct?
options: Deferred cancellation is acted on at defined cancellation points
Cleanup handlers can release resources during cancellation
Asynchronous cancellation can interrupt an invariant midway
Cancellation guarantees rollback of shared writes
answer: Deferred cancellation is acted on at defined cancellation points
Cleanup handlers can release resources during cancellation
Asynchronous cancellation can interrupt an invariant midway
questions.explanation: Deferred cancellation provides controlled interruption points, and cleanup can release locks. Asynchronous cancellation is risky; cancellation does not roll back writes.

questions.prompt: Which statements about fork from a multithreaded process are correct under typical POSIX semantics?
options: Only the calling thread exists in the child
The child has a separate process identity
The child may call exec to start a clean program image
All sibling threads continue running inside the child
answer: Only the calling thread exists in the child
The child has a separate process identity
The child may call exec to start a clean program image
questions.explanation: The child is a new process, but only the calling thread remains after fork. Exec is a common safe next step; sibling threads are not duplicated as active threads.

questions.prompt: Which can cause a thread to stop executing temporarily without terminating?
options: Preemption
Blocking on I/O
Waiting for a mutex
Returning from the thread start routine
answer: Preemption
Blocking on I/O
Waiting for a mutex
questions.explanation: Preemption, I/O waits, and lock waits suspend execution while preserving the thread. Returning from the start routine normally terminates that thread.

questions.prompt: Which statements about parallel speedup are correct?
options: A serial fraction limits achievable speedup
A global lock can serialize otherwise parallel work
More threads always guarantee lower completion time
CPU and memory contention can reduce gains
answer: A serial fraction limits achievable speedup
A global lock can serialize otherwise parallel work
CPU and memory contention can reduce gains
questions.explanation: Serial work and contention limit speedup. Adding threads can increase overhead or contention, so it does not always reduce completion time.

questions.prompt: Which are properties of a data race in the usual shared-memory model?
options: Conflicting accesses occur without adequate synchronization
At least one access is a write
Two reads alone constitute a data race
A race can make behavior unpredictable
answer: Conflicting accesses occur without adequate synchronization
At least one access is a write
A race can make behavior unpredictable
questions.explanation: A race involves unsynchronized conflicting accesses, at least one of which writes. Concurrent reads do not conflict, while a race can yield unpredictable outcomes.

questions.prompt: Which statements about thread-local storage are correct?
options: Each thread has a distinct instance
It can avoid synchronization for per-thread state
It makes all global variables private
Its instances are shared across processes automatically
answer: Each thread has a distinct instance
It can avoid synchronization for per-thread state
questions.explanation: Thread-local variables provide per-thread instances and can eliminate races on that particular state. They do not privatize ordinary globals or automatically share across processes.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a barrier are correct?
options: It coordinates a fixed group at a phase boundary
A participant can wait until the required arrivals occur
A missing participant can prevent release
A barrier itself protects every shared variable from races
answer: It coordinates a fixed group at a phase boundary
A participant can wait until the required arrivals occur
A missing participant can prevent release
questions.explanation: A barrier synchronizes arrival at a phase boundary. It does not provide mutual exclusion or protect data accesses by itself.

questions.prompt: Thread X increments a counter while holding mutex L. Thread Y uses a different mutex M to read the same counter. Is the read protected from the update?
options: No; both operations must use a common synchronization discipline
Yes; any mutex protects all shared data
Yes; the kernel serializes reads and writes
No, because threads cannot share counters
answer: No; both operations must use a common synchronization discipline
questions.explanation: The write is protected only against threads acquiring L. A reader using M can race because the two locks do not coordinate with one another.

questions.prompt: A program launches 100 threads for 100 tiny tasks. Why might this be slower than using a smaller worker pool?
options: Thread creation and scheduling overhead can outweigh useful work
More threads always reduce cache misses
The OS must serialize all threads
Threads cannot execute short tasks
answer: Thread creation and scheduling overhead can outweigh useful work
questions.explanation: For tiny tasks, managing many threads can cost more than the computation. A bounded pool amortizes setup and reduces scheduling overhead.

questions.prompt: A process has two threads and one thread calls exit_group-like process termination. What happens to the other thread?
options: It terminates as part of process-wide termination
It continues with a private process image
It becomes the new parent
It is guaranteed to finish its current function
answer: It terminates as part of process-wide termination
questions.explanation: Process-wide termination ends all threads in the process; thread-specific exit would be needed to end only the caller.

questions.prompt: Thread A waits on a semaphore while Thread B signals it. What is the key difference from a condition variable if the signal happens before A waits?
options: The semaphore permit can be retained
The condition variable retains the signal instead
Both notifications are always lost
A is terminated
answer: The semaphore permit can be retained
questions.explanation: A semaphore maintains a count, so the signal increments a permit that a later wait can consume. A condition variable does not generally store notifications.

questions.prompt: A thread acquires a lock, updates shared state, then releases it. A second thread later acquires the same lock. What ordering property is commonly provided?
options: The first thread?s protected writes become visible to the second after lock handoff
The second thread sees a random old copy
The process forks at unlock
The lock guarantees disk persistence
answer: The first thread?s protected writes become visible to the second after lock handoff
questions.explanation: Synchronization operations typically establish memory-ordering/visibility between critical sections. They do not imply process creation or durable storage.

questions.prompt: On a two-core machine, two threads each run a CPU-bound loop with no shared lock. Which statement is possible?
options: They can execute simultaneously on separate cores
They must alternate on one core
They share one program counter
One must be a process
answer: They can execute simultaneously on separate cores
questions.explanation: With two available cores and independent runnable kernel-schedulable threads, the OS can run them in parallel.

questions.prompt: A thread is ready but not running because all CPUs are occupied. Is it blocked?
options: No; it is ready and waiting for CPU service
Yes; it is blocked on a device
Yes; it has terminated
No; it must be a user thread
answer: No; it is ready and waiting for CPU service
questions.explanation: A runnable thread awaiting CPU assignment is ready. Blocking means waiting for a specific event such as I/O, not merely for an available CPU.

questions.prompt: A process with one thread uses a user-level thread package. The package creates 20 user threads but no kernel threads. What does the kernel directly schedule?
options: The process?s single kernel execution context
Each of the 20 user threads separately
The shared heap
The user-level ready queue
answer: The process?s single kernel execution context
questions.explanation: Without kernel-thread support, the kernel knows only the underlying execution context. The user runtime multiplexes its 20 threads internally.

questions.prompt: A condition variable wait returns with the mutex reacquired. What should the thread do before using the protected resource?
options: Recheck the condition predicate
Unlock and assume it is true
Call fork
Clear the mutex state manually
answer: Recheck the condition predicate
questions.explanation: The wakeup does not promise the predicate remains true. Rechecking while holding the reacquired mutex protects correct use of the resource.

questions.prompt: A thread waits for a lock while the lock holder is blocked waiting for the waiter to signal a condition. What design error is most likely?
options: A circular wait/deadlock
False sharing
Thread-local storage
Copy-on-write
answer: A circular wait/deadlock
questions.explanation: Each thread is waiting for an action from the other while holding or requiring a resource, producing a circular dependency and deadlock.

questions.prompt: A worker thread pool has 5 threads. One worker blocks on I/O, while four tasks are queued. How many workers remain available to take queued work?
questions.explanation: One of five workers is blocked, leaving four that can potentially take queued tasks. Throughput may change when the blocked worker resumes.

questions.prompt: A process uses a mutex for a critical section that performs a 2-second network read. What is the main concern?
options: The lock is held across a long blocking operation, delaying other threads
The mutex becomes a semaphore
The network read is automatically canceled
The process address space is duplicated
answer: The lock is held across a long blocking operation, delaying other threads
questions.explanation: Holding a mutex across blocking I/O can prevent other threads needing that lock from progressing for a long time. Critical sections should generally avoid such waits.

questions.prompt: A thread releases a mutex it does not own. What can be concluded?
options: The operation violates normal mutex ownership rules and may fail or be undefined
It transfers ownership reliably
It wakes all threads and grants the lock to each
It is equivalent to signaling a condition variable
answer: The operation violates normal mutex ownership rules and may fail or be undefined
questions.explanation: Mutexes are ownership-based; unlocking from a non-owner is invalid under common APIs, though exact error behavior depends on mutex type and interface.

questions.prompt: A process creates 3 threads and then the initial thread returns from main. What is the process outcome?
options: In common process semantics, returning from main terminates the process and its threads
The other threads always continue until completion
The initial thread becomes a child
The process is necessarily suspended
answer: In common process semantics, returning from main terminates the process and its threads
questions.explanation: Returning from the process entry point commonly invokes process termination, ending all remaining threads. An explicit thread-exit operation is needed if they should continue.

questions.prompt: Which best describes a thread control block?
options: Per-thread metadata such as saved registers, state, and scheduling information
The shared process heap
A copy of the executable for every thread
A disk block containing the thread?s output
answer: Per-thread metadata such as saved registers, state, and scheduling information
questions.explanation: The TCB stores state needed to schedule and resume a thread. Shared address-space regions are process resources rather than per-thread control records.

questions.prompt: A shared counter is updated by atomic increments, but a thread performs a separate read followed by a decision and write. Is the whole sequence atomic?
options: No; only the atomic increment operation is indivisible
Yes; one atomic operation makes all later accesses atomic
Yes, if the thread has higher priority
No; atomic operations cannot update counters
answer: No; only the atomic increment operation is indivisible
questions.explanation: Atomicity applies to the specific operation, not an arbitrary multi-instruction sequence around it. The larger check-and-act sequence needs its own synchronization.

questions.prompt: Threads A and B both lock mutex M, but A unlocks it before updating the shared variable. What is true of the update?
options: The update is outside the protected critical section and may race
It remains protected because A previously held M
The scheduler delays B until after the update
The variable is converted to thread-local
answer: The update is outside the protected critical section and may race
questions.explanation: Mutual exclusion covers only code executed while holding the lock. Releasing it before the write leaves the write unsynchronized.

questions.prompt: Two threads are both runnable on a one-core machine. Can they be concurrent?
options: Yes, by interleaving execution over time
No, concurrency requires two cores
Yes, only if they share no memory
No, the scheduler can run only one thread total
answer: Yes, by interleaving execution over time
questions.explanation: A single CPU can interleave execution so both tasks make progress during overlapping intervals. Simultaneous execution would require multiple cores.

questions.prompt: A runtime uses many-to-many mapping with 6 kernel threads and 20 user threads on a 4-CPU machine. What bounds simultaneous execution?
options: At most 4 threads
At most 6 threads
At most 20 threads
At most 26 threads
answer: At most 4 threads
questions.explanation: Both the number of kernel execution contexts and CPUs constrain concurrency. min(6,4) = 4 can execute simultaneously.

questions.prompt: A thread blocks on a mutex in a kernel-supported threading model. What does the scheduler typically do?
options: It can schedule another runnable thread
It must idle the CPU
It converts the mutex owner into a process
It copies the blocked thread?s stack
answer: It can schedule another runnable thread
questions.explanation: A blocked thread is not runnable, but other kernel-schedulable threads can use the CPU. The scheduler need not idle if work remains.
